title: Swimming strokes for hip arthritis
meta_title: Swimming for Hip Arthritis: Stroke Choice and Safety
meta_description: Choose swimming or water exercise that suits your hip arthritis. Practical pool access checks, evidence limits, safer pacing and when to get help.
excerpt: No one swimming stroke suits everyone with hip arthritis. Plan pool access, adapt painful movements and learn how swimming differs from aquatic physiotherapy.
direct_answer: There is no single swimming stroke that suits everyone with hip osteoarthritis. Choose a comfortable activity and adapt any movement that causes pain. If changing the activity does not help, end the session and seek advice. A physiotherapist or swimming teacher can help you find an appropriate starting point.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: swimming exercises hip osteoarthritis, aquatic exercise hip oa, water exercises hip arthritis

citations.label: Swim England: musculoskeletal conditions and swimming
Cochrane: aquatic exercise for knee or hip osteoarthritis (2016)

content:
Quick answer: There is no single swimming stroke that suits everyone with hip osteoarthritis. Choose a stroke or water activity you can do comfortably and safely. If a movement causes pain, stop that movement and try an easier option; if pain continues, end the session and seek advice. A physiotherapist or qualified swimming teacher can help you adapt your technique.

Swimming lengths and aquatic physiotherapy are different activities. You do not need to swim lengths to benefit from exercising in water. This guide helps you plan a safer first visit, choose questions for a physiotherapist and understand what the evidence can and cannot tell you. It is general information, not a personal exercise or post-operative rehabilitation plan.

Which swimming stroke should I choose?

Swim England's guidance for musculoskeletal conditions recommends finding a stroke or variation that works for you, rather than naming one stroke as best for every painful hip. Your shoulders, neck, confidence in water and swimming technique matter too.

  • Backstroke: it may suit you, but do not assume it is automatically the gentlest choice. If it brings on pain elsewhere, ask about a different stroke or technique.
  • Front crawl: use a comfortable technique rather than trying to complete a set distance through pain. A swimming teacher can help if breathing or body position is difficult.
  • Breaststroke: if the kick causes hip, groin or knee pain, stop that movement. Ask a teacher or physiotherapist about an alternative instead of forcing a wider kick.
  • Not comfortable swimming lengths? Ask about supported water walking or a supervised aquatic exercise session. Being unable to swim does not rule out aquatic physiotherapy.

What does exercising in water offer?

Water supports some of your body weight and provides resistance to movement. Warm-water aquatic physiotherapy, also called hydrotherapy, uses exercises tailored to your needs. It is not the same as a general swim or a vigorous aqua-aerobics class. Arthritis UK's hydrotherapy information explains what a supervised session involves.

A 2016 Cochrane review found small, short-term improvements in pain and disability after aquatic exercise programmes for groups with knee or hip osteoarthritis. The review searched trials up to April 2015. It did not establish a winning swimming stroke or show that swimming repairs cartilage. Results from a supervised exercise programme should not be presented as a guarantee about casual swimming lengths.

NICE recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to the person, including strengthening and general fitness. Some discomfort can occur when starting exercise. This does not mean you should push through sharp pain, a movement that is clearly worsening symptoms or a new injury.

Plan the first visit before getting in

  1. Check access. Ask about steps, a rail, a hoist and accessible changing facilities. Think about getting out when you are tired, not only getting in.
  2. Choose the right session. Ask whether there are quieter sessions, adult lessons or supervised sessions suitable for your needs. Pool temperatures and depths differ.
  3. Start with what you can manage. Do not copy a fixed number of lengths or repetitions from someone else's programme. A physiotherapist can help set a starting point and progression.
  4. Tell the instructor what is difficult. Explain which movements bring on pain and whether you need help with balance, confidence or entry to the pool.

Water walking and other pool exercises

Water walking can be an alternative to swimming. Ask an instructor or physiotherapist to show you an appropriate depth and support. Exercises such as side stepping or moving the hip through a comfortable range may form part of an individual programme, but this page does not prescribe a universal set of hip circles, leg lifts or repetitions.

Build up gradually. If a movement causes pain, stop that movement and, if comfortable, try something easier. If that does not help, end the session and seek advice before exercising again. Some tiredness or muscle aching afterwards can happen; excessive symptoms are a reason to reduce the next session and discuss your plan.

When to check suitability first

Tell the physiotherapist or pool team about wounds, skin infection, fever, recent illness, heart or breathing problems, or a condition that is not well controlled. These can affect whether the session is suitable or what support is needed. Do not treat this list as a medical clearance checklist.

After a hip replacement: follow your own surgical and physiotherapy team's instructions about returning to the pool, wound healing and permitted movements. This osteoarthritis guide is not clearance to swim after surgery, and a date from another person's recovery plan may not apply to you.

When hip pain needs urgent help

Following NHS hip-pain advice, call 999 or go to A&E for severe hip pain after a fall or injury, inability to walk or put weight on your leg, or tingling or loss of feeling after an injury. Do not drive yourself to A&E.

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for severe hip pain that starts suddenly without an injury, a hot swollen hip, skin colour change around the hip, or hip pain with fever or feeling generally unwell. Do not wait for a swimming session to see whether it settles.

Useful next steps

Use our osteoarthritis guide for the wider care picture, hip-exercise information for related land-based movement, the exercise hub for more movement information and aquatic-therapy guide for more context. These are educational resources, not substitutes for your own care plan.
